sec.title: Background
sec.p: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is a common oral cavity malignancy with a poor prognosis. Although chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1) has been implicated in tumor progression in several types of cancer, its role and underlying mechanisms in OSCC remain unclear. In this study, we examined the role and mitochondrial metabolism pattern of CMKLR1 in OSCC progression.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: CMKLR1 expression was evaluated using data obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas database and from immunohistochemical, RT-qPCR, and Western blotting analyses involving OSCC tissues and cell lines. Functional assays focusing on proliferation, migration, invasion, and colony formation were conducted after CMKLR1 knockdown or overexpression in OSCC cells. Proteomic analyses were conducted to identify CMKLR1-associated signaling pathways. Seahorse assays were used to assess mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). In addition, the effect of mitochondrial inhibition with IACS-010759 was evaluated in CMKLR1-overexpressing models. Finally, signaling dependency was tested through PI3K/AKT inhibition and PGC-1α depletion.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: CMKLR1 expression was significantly elevated in OSCC, correlating with advanced OSCC, lymph node metastasis, and poor prognosis. CMKLR1 knockdown inhibited cell proliferation, migration, invasion, and epithelial‐to‐mesenchymal transition in vitro and suppressed tumor growth in vivo, whereas CMKLR1 overexpression had the opposite effect. Proteomic profiling and metabolic assays revealed that CMKLR1 knockdown suppressed mitochondrial function, decreased OXPHOS activity, and reduced ATP production. Additionally, pharmacological inhibition of OXPHOS with IACS-010759 significantly abrogated the tumor-promoting effects driven by CMKLR1 overexpression, thereby supporting a CMKLR1-OXPHOS regulatory axis in OSCC. Mechanistically, CMKLR1 activated PI3K/AKT signaling and induced PGC-1α production. Pharmacological blockade of PI3K/AKT abrogated CMKLR1-dependent PGC-1α upregulation, and PGC-1α depletion attenuated CMKLR1-driven mitochondrial respiration.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: CMKLR1 is a novel driver of OXPHOS in OSCC that functions through the PI3K/AKT/PGC-1α axis. Targeting mitochondrial metabolism may represent a promising therapeutic strategy for patients with overexpression of CMKLR1 and OSCC.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is one of the most common malignancies of the oral and maxillofacial region and is characterized by high local invasiveness and frequent cervical lymph node metastasis.1 For many years, the 5-year survival rate of patients with advanced OSCC has remained suboptimal, largely because of late diagnosis, recurrence, and distant metastasis.2 Surgical resection often results in complex defects that are challenging to reconstruct and that can lead to substantial functional impairment, delayed wound healing, and postoperative complications. These clinical challenges highlight an urgent need for identification of molecular targets that can be used to establish novel therapeutic strategies beyond conventional surgery and radiotherapy.

Metabolic reprogramming is a hallmark of cancer that plays a key role in tumor development and progression.3, 4, 5 For decades, research in this field has predominantly focused on aerobic glycolysis, also known as the Warburg effect, as the primary metabolic feature of cancer cells. However, accumulating evidence suggests that mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) also substantially contributes to energy production in various tumor types,6,7 including OSCC.8 OXPHOS is a mitochondrial process that generates ATP by oxidizing nutrients through the electron transport chain.9 Contrary to the earlier assumption that mitochondrial respiration is broadly suppressed in cancer, many tumors have been reported to exhibit elevated OXPHOS activity, which has been linked to aggressive behavior and therapy resistance in breast cancer, leukemia, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma.10,11 According to the literature, targeting OXPHOS by using small-molecule inhibitors has therapeutic potential with respect to overcoming resistance to targeted therapies and chemotherapy.12 However, the mechanism underlying the regulation of OXPHOS in OSCC remains poorly understood.

Chemokine-like receptor 1 (CMKLR1), also known as ChemR23, is a G-protein-coupled receptor activated by chemerin and resolvin E1 that has been implicated in inflammation, immune regulation, and tumor biology.13,14 Multiple studies have suggested that CMKLR1 can promote cancer cell proliferation, invasion, and metastasis through diverse signaling pathways, including DLL4-Notch, NF-κB, and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, in various malignancies such as adrenocortical carcinoma, colorectal cancer, glioma, breast cancer, and prostate cancer.13,15, 16, 17 However, the relevance of CMKLR1 to OSCC remains incompletely understood. In our previous studies on the role of the chemerin/CMKLR1 axis in OSCC, we reported that elevated chemerin is associated with aggressive clinicopathological features and that chemerin promotes OSCC cell motility through CMKLR1-dependent signaling.13,18 In the present study, we focused on the tumor-cell-intrinsic role of the receptor CMKLR1 and examined whether this ligand couples receptor signaling to mitochondrial bioenergetics, which is an axis that has increasingly been implicated in invasion and therapy tolerance in OSCC. Clarifying this connection would extend the understanding of the biology of CMKLR1 beyond descriptive phenotypes and may reveal a mechanistically grounded, therapeutically exploitable metabolic dependency.

In this study, we examined the function of CMKLR1 in OSCC and whether CMKLR1 drives OSCC aggressiveness by rewiring mitochondrial bioenergetics. By integrating analyses of patient samples, cell models, and functional assays, we explored whether CMKLR1 contributes to OSCC progression through mitochondrial metabolism modulation.

sec.title: Patient samples and public data
sec.p: We retrospectively screened the data of patients with histologically confirmed primary OSCC who underwent surgical resection at First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University between 2016 and 2019. Patients were considered eligible for inclusion in the analysis if they had pathologically confirmed OSCC and complete clinicopathological and follow-up data. Patients were excluded if they had undergone preoperative neoadjuvant therapy, had recurrent disease at presentation, or had an incomplete record. All eligible cases identified within the predefined period were collected. The sample size was determined through tissue availability and tissue microarray construction feasibility. A total of 50 OSCC frozen specimens and paired adjacent noncancerous tissues were obtained for reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR). Additionally, five pairs of OSCC tissues and paired adjacent noncancerous tissues were obtained for Western blots. Additionally, an OSCC tissue microarray comprising 68 paired OSCC and matched adjacent non-tumor tissues with follow-up data was employed for prognostic analysis. Clinical data and follow-up information, including overall survival (OS) were recorded. OS was defined as the time from surgical resection to death or the last follow-up. These records were used to analyze the correlation between CMKLR1 expression and patient prognosis. Transcriptomic data obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database (https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/) were analyzed to examine the expression patterns of CMKLR1 in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) and to evaluate its association with clinicopathological parameters and patient survival. This study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the First Affiliated Hospital of Sun Yat-sen University (approval number: 2017173).

sec.title: Cell culture, lentiviral infection, and small interfering RNA transfection
sec.p: The human OSCC cell lines Cal-27 and SCC-9 were obtained from the Cell Bank of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (Shanghai, China). Cells were cultured in either Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (Gibco, Waltham, MA, USA) or Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium combined with Ham’s F-12 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin solution (Gibco). All cells were maintained at 37 °C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO2. For inhibitor treatment, cells were treated with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 (10μM, HY-10108, MCE) or IACS-010759 (100nM, S8731; Selleck Chemicals）, with matched DMSO used as vehicle control.

Short hairpin RNA (shRNA) lentiviral vectors targeting human CMKLR1 were purchased from OBiO Technology (Shanghai, China). Lentiviral particles encoding full-length human CMKLR1 cDNA (vector name: GV358, OE-CMKLR1) were purchased from GeneChem Technology (Shanghai, China). CMKLR1-overexpressing stable cell lines were generated in SCC-9 cells. Transduction was performed in the presence of 8 μg/mL polybrene (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) followed by puromycin selection (2 μg/mL) to generate stably expressing clones.
The following are the shRNA sequences used in this study:
CMKLR1-shRNA#1 Forward:5’-CCggGGTGATGAATACCCTGATTCTCAAGAGAAATCAGGGTATTCATCACCTTTTTTg-3’;
Reverse:5’-aattCaaaaaaGGTGATGAATACCCTGATTTCTCTTGAgAATCAGGGTATTCATCACC-3’
CMKLR1-shRNA#2: Forward:5’-CCggGCAACTTCCTTCTCATCCATTCAAGAGATGGATGAGAAGGAAGTTGCTTTTTTg-3’.
Reverse:5’-aattcaaaaaaGCAACTTCCTTCTCATCCATCTCTTGAATGGATGAGAAGGAAGTTGC-3’.

Transient PGC-1α knockdown was performed using small interfering RNA (siRNA) targeting human PPARGC1A (siPGC-1α, forward: GCUCCAAGACUCUAGACAATT, reverse: UUGUCUAGAGUCUUGGAGCTT) and nontargeting control siRNA (siNC, forward: UUCUCCGAACGUGUCACGUTT, reverse: ACGUGACACGUUCGGAGAATT), synthesized by RiboBio (Guangzhou, China). Cells were then transfected with Lipofectamine RNAiMAX (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, cells were seeded to reach 50% to 60% confluence on the day of transfection, and siRNAs were used at a final concentration of 20 to 50 nM. Subsequently, knockdown efficiency was validated 48 hours after transfection through either Western blotting or RT-qPCR or both.

sec.title: RNA extraction and RT-qPCR
sec.p: Total RNA was extracted from OSCC frozen tissues and cells by using specific kits (GOONIE, China). Reverse transcription was performed using a High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (4368813; Thermo Fisher Scientific). RT-qPCR was then performed using the SYBR Green Master Mix (Yeasen, China) on a Real-Time PCR System (biorad, CA). Quantification was performed using the 2−ΔΔCT method. The following are the sequences of the primers used: CMKLR1 (forward: GCCAACCTGCATGGGAAAATA, reverse: GTGAGGTAGCAAGCTGTGATG), ACTB (forward: CATGTACGTTGCTATCCAGGC, reverse: CTCCTTAATGTCACGCACGAT), PPARGC1A (forward: TCTGAGTCTGTATGGAGTGACAT, reverse: CCAAGTCGTTCACATCTAGTTCA).

sec.title: Western blots
sec.p: Total protein was extracted from OSCC cells and tissue samples by using RIPA lysis buffer (Beyotime, Shanghai, China) supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein were separated through 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and transferred onto polyvinylidene difluoride membranes (Millipore, Burlington, MA, USA). These membranes were then blocked with 5% blocking buffer in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween 20 for 1 hour at room temperature, with this followed by overnight incubation at 4 °C with primary antibodies against CMKLR1 (#ab306554; Abcam, Cambridge, UK), β-actin (#P30002; Abmart, Shanghai, China), E-cadherin (#610181; BD Biosciences, Shanghai, China), N-cadherin (#13116; Cell Signaling Technology, Danvers, MA, USA), vimentin (#5741; Cell Signaling Technology), Snail (#3879; Cell Signaling Technology), Slug (#9585; Cell Signaling Technology), PI3K (#AF6241; Affinity Biosciences, Cincinnati, OH, USA), PGC1 (#AF5395; Affinity Biosciences), Phospho-PI3K (#AF3241; Affinity Biosciences), and OXPHOS Cocktail (#PK30006; Proteintech, Rosemont, IL, USA). After the membranes were washed, they were incubated with secondary antibodies conjugated to horseradish peroxidase (#ab6721; Abcam and #31430; Invitrogen) for 1 hour at room temperature. Finally, protein bands were visualized using enhanced chemiluminescence reagents (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA, USA).

sec.title: Cell counting Kit-8 assay
sec.p: Cell proliferation was assessed using a Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; Dojindo, Kumamoto, Japan) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, stably transfected cells (1000 cells/well) with 100 μL medium were seeded onto 96-well plates overnight. At the time of analysis, 10 μL CCK-8 reagent was added to each well, and the mixture was incubated for 2 hours at 37 °C. Finally, absorbance was measured at 450 nm by using a microplate reader (Bio-Rad Laboratories).

sec.title: Colony formation assay
sec.p: Briefly, 1 × 103 stably transfected cells were seeded onto six-well plates. The cells were incubated for 2 weeks until visible colonies appeared, and they were then gently washed with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 minutes at room temperature, and stained with 0.1% crystal violet (Beyotime) for 30 minutes. Colonies containing more than 50 cells were counted under a light microscope and photographed.

sec.title: Immunohistochemical (IHC) staining
sec.p: An immunohistochemical (IHC) staining assay was conducted as described in a previous study.19 Briefly, tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through graded ethanol solutions. Antigens were then repaired by microwaving them in 10 mmol/L citrate buffer at pH 6.0 for 15 minutes. Subsequently, the sections were incubated with 3% H2O2 for 15 minutes to block endogenous peroxidase, with this followed by blocking with 5% bovine serum albumin at 37 °C for 30 minutes. Next, the slides were incubated overnight at 4 °C with a primary antibody against CMKLR1 (dilution 1:200, ab306554; Abcam) or Ki67 (ab15580; Abcam). After three washes with PBS, the sections were incubated with a horseradish-peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (1:5000, ab6721; Abcam) for 30 minutes at room temperature. Finally, immunoreactivity was visualized using a DAB substrate kit (ZSGB-Bio, Beijing, China), and nuclei were counterstained with hematoxylin.

IHC staining was independently evaluated by two experienced pathologists in a blinded manner. After the intensity of staining (0 = negative, 1 = weak, 2 = moderate, and 3 = strong) and the percentage of positively stained cells were calculated, 0 (0%-10%), 1 (11%-25%), 2 (26%-75%), 3 (76%-100%), and an immunoreactivity score was calculated by multiplying these two values. This score ranged from 0 to 9 points, with a score of ≥6 indicating high CMKLR1 expression and a score of <6 indicating low or no CMKLR1 expression.

sec.title: Xenograft mouse model
sec.p: BALB/c nude mice (female, 4-5 weeks old, weighing between 18 and 20 g) were purchased from Guangdong Medical Laboratory Animal Center and housed under specific-pathogen-free conditions (12 hours light/dark cycle). A total of 1 × 10⁷OSCC cells, including CMKLR1-overexpressing cells, CMKLR1-knockdown cells, and their corresponding control cells, were suspended in 100 μL of PBS/Matrigel (v/v = 2:1) and subcutaneously injected into the mice’s flanks (n = 6 per group). The mice were then monitored three times per week. Tumor growth was monitored twice a week. Tumor length (L) and width (W) were measured using calipers, and tumor volume was calculated as V = (L × W2)/2. A subset of mice bearing CMKLR1-overexpressing tumors were randomly divided into two groups (n = 5 per group, randomly allocated) and treated with the OXPHOS inhibitor IACS-010759 (5 mg/kg/day, intragastric, S8731; Selleck Chemicals, Houston, TX, USA) for 10 consecutive days, starting on day 5 after tumor implantation. After the mice were sacrificed, their tumors were measured, weighed, and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for IHC analysis. All animal procedures were approved by the Animal Research Ethics Committee of the Guangzhou Medical University (Approval No. G2022-117).

sec.title: Transwell assays
sec.p: Transwell assays were conducted using 24-well Transwell chambers (8-μm pores; BD Biosciences). After OSCC cells were trypsinized and resuspended in serum-free medium, a 200-μL fraction was seeded into the upper chamber at a density of 1 × 105 cells/well. The lower chamber was then filled with 600 μL of medium containing 10% fetal bovine serum as a chemoattractant. After incubation at 37°C for 24 to 36 hours, noninvading cells on the upper surface of the membrane were removed using a cotton swab, and invading cells on the lower surface of the membrane were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde for 20 minutes and stained with 0.1% crystal violet for 30 minutes. Finally, five random fields per membrane were imaged and counted under a light microscope.

sec.title: Proteome sequencing
sec.p: All proteomic analyses were conducted by GeneChem (Shanghai, China). Total protein was extracted from CMKLR1-knockdown Cal-27 cells and corresponding control cells by using RIPA lysis buffer containing protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Beyotime). Protein concentrations were determined using a BCA Protein Assay Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Equal amounts of protein from each sample were digested with trypsin through a filter-aided sample preparation protocol. Peptides were desalted using C18 columns and labeled with tandem mass tag reagents (Thermo Fisher Scientific) in accordance with the manufacturer’ s instructions. Peptides labeled by a tandem mass tag were fractionated through reversed-phase chromatography on an Agilent 1260 Infinity II HPLC system and analyzed using a Q Exactive Plus mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled to an EASY-nLC system (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Raw tandem mass spectrometry data were processed using the MASCOT engine (version 2.6; Matrix Science, London, UK) embedded into Proteome Discoverer 2.2. Differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) were identified on the basis of a fold change threshold of >1.2 or <0.83 and a P value of <.05. Finally, bioinformatic analyses including Gene Ontology (GO), Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment, and subcellular localization analyses were conducted.

sec.title: Seahorse assay
sec.p: Mitochondrial respiration was examined using a Seahorse XF Cell Mito Stress Test Kit (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA) in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, OSCC cells were seeded onto Seahorse XF96 microplates at a density of 1 × 104 cells/well and incubated overnight. Before the assay, the cells were washed and incubated in Seahorse XF Base Medium at 37 °C in a non-CO2-containing incubator for 1 hour. Subsequently, oxygen consumption rate (OCR) measurements were conducted using a Seahorse XFe96 Analyzer (Agilent Technologies) under basal conditions, with this followed by the sequential injection of the following mitochondrial stressors: 1 μM oligomycin (ATP synthase inhibitor), 1.5 μM FCCP (mitochondrial uncoupler), and 0.5 μM rotenone/antimycin A (complex I/III inhibitors). Data were then normalized to protein concentration per well and analyzed using Wave software (Agilent Technologies). Parameters such as basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity were calculated in accordance with standard protocols. Finally, ATP production rates were calculated from OCR measurements.

sec.title: MitoTracker staining and quantification
sec.p: Cells were incubated with MitoTracker Red CMXRos (200 nM, Beyotime Biotechnology, China) at 37 °C for 30 minutes, washed with PBS, and analyzed under a confocal laser scanning microscope (Carl Zeiss, Oberkochen, Germany). Fluorescence intensity was quantified using ImageJ software, with at least five randomly selected fields per condition.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: All statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics, version 20.0 (IBM, Armonk, NY, USA). Quantitative data are presented as mean ± standard deviation values. Multiple sets of quantitative data were analyzed through one-way analysis of variance, and pairwise comparisons were conducted using Tukey’s post hoc method. Survival curves were plotted using the Kaplan–Meier survival method and compared through a log-rank test. Univariate Cox proportional-hazards regression models were used to conduct a univariate analysis of the impact of CMKLR1 expression on OS. All in vitro experiments were conducted at least three times. All statistical tests were two-sided, with a P value of <.05 considered significant.

sec.title: CMKLR1 is upregulated in OSCC and is associated with a poor prognosis
sec.p:
To explore the potential role of CMKLR1 in OSCC, TCGA database was used to analyze the expression of CMKLR1 in HNSCC tissues. The results indicated that CMKLR1 mRNA was significantly upregulated in HNSCC compared with adjacent normal tissues (Figure 1A). Patients with lymph node metastasis exhibited higher CMKLR1 expression compared with those without metastasis (Figure 1B). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed that higher CMKLR1 expression was significantly associated with poorer OS in patients with HNSCC (Figure 1C).Fig. 1
CMKLR1 is overexpressed in OSCC and is associated with a poor prognosis. Relative mRNA expression of CMKLR1 in (A) HNSCC tissues (n = 520) versus adjacent normal tissues (n = 44) and in (B) non–lymph node (N0) versus lymph node (N1) samples, according to TCGA database analysis. (C) Kaplan–Meier survival analysis of OS based on CMKLR1 expression in patients with HNSCC, with data from TCGA. (D) Representative IHC images depicting CMKLR1 expression in OSCC tissues and adjacent normal oral mucosal tissues (n = 68). Scale bar = 20 μm. (E) Quantitative analysis of CMKLR1 IHC staining intensity in OSCC samples (n = 68) versus normal tissue samples, with subgroup comparisons based on T stage, clinical stage, and lymph node metastasis. (F) Kaplan–Meier survival analysis of patients with OSCC with high versus low CMKLR1 expression according to IHC scores. (G) RT-qPCR analysis of CMKLR1 mRNA expression in 50 paired OSCC and adjacent normal tissues. (H) Western blot analysis of CMKLR1 protein levels in five representative paired OSCC (T) and adjacent nontumorous (N) tissues. N, adjacent nontumorous tissues; T, OSCC tumor tissues; TCGA, The Cancer Genome Atlas. *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 1 dummy alt text

To validate the aforementioned findings, an IHC analysis was conducted on tissue microarrays containing 68 paired OSCC and adjacent non-tumor tissues. The results indicated that the protein levels of CMKLR1 were significantly elevated in the OSCC tissues (Figures 1D). Clinicopathological correlation analysis revealed that high CMKLR1 expression was significantly associated with advanced T stage (P = .035), clinical stage (P = .002), and lymph node metastasis (P = .003), but not with patient age, sex, or tumor differentiation (Table). Analysis of CMKLR1 mRNA expression in 50 paired OSCC and adjacent nontumorous tissues revealed consistently increased CMKLR1 mRNA expression in tumor tissues (Figure 1G). Western blotting of five paired OSCC and adjacent tissues further confirmed that the protein levels of CMKLR1 were significantly higher in the OSCC samples than in the normal control group (Figure 1H). Taken together, these findings indicate that CMKLR1 is often upregulated in OSCC and may serve as a biomarker of poor clinical outcomes.

sec.title: CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell proliferation and tumor growth in vivo
sec.p:
To examine the biological role of CMKLR1 in the progression of OSCC, we established CMKLR1-knockdown Cal-27 cells (Sh) and CMKLR1-overexpressing SCC-9 cells (OE). Western blot and RT-qPCR confirmed the efficiency of CMKLR1 silencing and overexpression in the respective cell lines (Figure 2A, Supplementary Figure S1). CCK-8 assays revealed that CMKLR1 downregulation significantly inhibited the proliferation of Cal-27 cells, whereas CMKLR1 overexpression enhanced the proliferation of SCC-9 cells (Figure 2B). Additionally, colony formation assays demonstrated that CMKLR1 knockdown reduced colony formation, whereas CMKLR1 overexpression increased the number of colonies formed (Figure 2C and D).Fig. 2
CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell proliferation and tumor growth in vivo. (A) Western blot analysis confirming CMKLR1 knockdown in Cal-27 cells (Sh1 and Sh2) and CMKLR1 overexpression in SCC-9 cells (OE). (B) CCK-8 proliferation assays of the proliferation of CMKLR1-silenced Cal-27 cells and CMKLR1-overexpressing SCC-9 cells. (C, D) Colony formation assays and quantification in the indicated groups. (E) Representative images of xenograft tumors derived from OSCC cells with CMKLR1 knockdown (Sh), OSCC cells with CMKLR1 overexpression (OE), and control cells (NC). (F) Tumor growth curves demonstrating tumor volume changes over time. (G) Tumor weight measurements at the endpoint. *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 2 dummy alt text

To further examine the role of CMKLR1 in vivo, subcutaneous xenograft experiments were conducted on nude mice. OSCC cells were subcutaneously injected into the right flanks of nude mice to establish an OSCC xenograft mouse model. Compared with those in the control group, the tumors derived from CMKLR1-overexpressing OSCC cells grew significantly faster and were larger in volume and weight. By contrast, tumors from CMKLR1-knockdown cells exhibited markedly slower growth and lower tumor burden (Figure 2E-G). Collectively, these findings indicate that CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell proliferation and tumorigenicity both in vivo and in vitro.

sec.title: CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell migration and invasion and induces epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition
sec.p:
We examined the role of CMKLR1 in OSCC cell migration and invasion by conducting wound healing and Transwell assays. Our results indicated that CMKLR1 knockdown significantly reduced the rate of wound closure in Cal-27 cells, whereas CMKLR1 overexpression enhanced the migration of SCC-9 cells (Figure 3A and B). Transwell invasion assays further revealed that CMKLR1 silencing markedly impaired the invasive capacity of OSCC cells, whereas CMKLR1 overexpression promoted their invasion (Figure 3C and D).Fig. 3
CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell migration, invasion, and EMT. Representative images and quantification of wound healing assays in (A) Cal-27 cells with CMKLR1 knockdown and (B) SCC-9 cells with CMKLR1 overexpression. Transwell invasion assays and quantification in (C) Cal-27 and (D) SCC-9 cells, revealing a decreased and increased invasive capacity after CMKLR1 knockdown and overexpression, respectively. Scale bar = 100 μm. (E) Western blot analysis of EMT markers (E-cadherin, N-cadherin, vimentin, Snail, and Slug) in CMKLR1-modified OSCC cells. *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 3 dummy alt text

Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) is a phenotypic program in which epithelial cells reduce cell-to-cell adhesion and acquire mesenchymal features that facilitate motility and invasion. Because of the pronounced changes we observed during migration and invasion, we assessed various EMT-associated markers, including E-cadherin as an epithelial adhesion marker and N-cadherin/vimentin as mesenchymal markers, as well as EMT-related transcription factors (Snail and Slug). Our results indicated the following. In CMKLR1-silenced Cal-27 cells, the epithelial marker E-cadherin was upregulated, whereas the mesenchymal markers N-cadherin, vimentin, Snail, and Slug were downregulated. By contrast, CMKLR1 overexpression in SCC-9 cells induced a mesenchymal phenotype, as reflected by reduced levels of E-cadherin and increased levels of N-cadherin, vimentin, and EMT-associated transcription factors (Figure 3E). Taken together, these findings indicate that CMKLR1 promotes OSCC cell migration, invasion, and EMT.

sec.title: CMKLR1 knockdown alters the mitochondrial metabolism of OSCC cells
sec.p:
To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying CMKLR1-mediated OSCC progression, we performed quantitative proteomic profiling on CMKLR1-knockdown Cal-27 cells. A total of 1618 DEPs (fold change > 1.2 or fold change <0.83, P < .05) were identified, of which 882 were upregulated and 736 were downregulated compared with the control group (Figure 4A). The heatmap of the top 20 upregulated and top 20 downregulated proteins revealed that the DEPs clustered by different samples in the two groups were uniform (Figure 4B). Additionally, subcellular localization analysis revealed that altered proteins were distributed across various compartments, including the nucleus (38.1%), cytosol (20.2%), plasma membrane (16.7%), extracellular space (10.3%), and mitochondria (11.9%) (Figure 4C). These findings suggested that CMKLR1 depletion was accompanied by broad remodeling of mitochondria-associated proteins. Next, we examined the top 10 significantly enriched GO terms, and we identified the pathway related to mitochondrial activity, including NADH dehydrogenase activity, NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) activity, and oxidoreductase activity, as the most enriched pathway (Figure 4D). KEGG pathway enrichment analysis revealed that oxidative phosphorylation was significantly enriched in CMKLR1-silenced cells (Figure 4E). Gene set enrichment analysis further revealed a reduction in mitochondrial respiratory activity after CMKLR1 knockdown (Figure 4F).Fig. 4
CMKLR1 knockdown suppresses mitochondrial OXPHOS in OSCC cells. (A) Volcano plot of DEPs in CMKLR1-knockdown and control Cal-27 cells, depicting upregulated proteins (red), downregulated proteins (blue), and nonsignificant proteins (gray). (B) Heatmap of the top DEPs identified through proteomic analysis. (C) Subcellular localization pie chart of DEPs, revealing a large proportion localized to mitochondria. (D, E) GO and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses of DEPs, highlighting enrichment in OXPHOS-related processes. (F) Gene set enrichment analysis demonstrating the significant downregulation of OXPHOS in CMKLR1-silenced cells. (G) Seahorse XF analysis of mitochondrial respiration indicating a reduced OCR in CMKLR1-knockdown OSCC cells. (H) Quantification of basal respiration, ATP production, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity in CMKLR1-knockdown cells. (I) Western blot analysis of representative OXPHOS complex subunits (CI-NDUFB8, CII-SDHB, CIII-UQCRC1, CIV-MTCO2, and CV-ATP5A1), with β-actin as loading control. (J) Representative MitoTracker images and quantification of fluorescence intensity (MitoTracker Red, scale bar = 20 μm). *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 4 dummy alt text

To functionally validate the aforementioned findings, we conducted a mitochondrial respiration assay by using a Seahorse XF analyzer. Our results indicated that CMKLR1 knockdown significantly reduced the overall OCR in OSCC cells (Figure 4G). Statistical analysis further revealed a significant reduction in basal respiration, maximal respiration, and ATP production in CMKLR1-depleted cells (Figure 4H). These results confirmed the impairment of mitochondrial OXPHOS. Moreover, immunoblotting of representative OXPHOS complex subunits spanning complexes I–V (CI-NDUFB8, CII-SDHB, CIII-UQCRC1, CIV-MTCO2, and CV-ATP5A1) revealed a reduction in OXPHOS protein abundance in CMKLR1-silenced cells (Figure 4I). Consistently, MitoTracker staining demonstrated reduced mitochondrial signal intensity after CMKLR1 knockdown (please refer to Figure 4J for the quantification results). Collectively, these findings confirm that CMKLR1 depletion suppresses mitochondrial oxidative metabolism in OSCC cells.

sec.title: CMKLR1 promotes OXPHOS and OSCC progression by activating the PI3K/AKT/PGC-1α axis
sec.p:
CMKLR1 is a G-protein-coupled receptor that can engage canonical growth and metabolic pathways. In this study, we explored the link between CMKLR1 signaling and mitochondrial bioenergetics. We focused on the PI3K/AKT pathway, a known downstream module of G-protein-coupled receptor signaling with an established role in metabolic adaptation. Immunoblotting revealed that CMKLR1 knockdown reduced the phosphorylation of PI3K and AKT (p-PI3K and p-AKT), with minimal changes observed in total PI3K and AKT abundance (Figure 5A). These findings suggested that CMKLR1 modulated the activation status of PI3K/AKT in OSCC cells. Because PI3K/AKT signaling can influence mitochondrial biogenesis and oxidative metabolism, we examined PGC-1α, a central transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial oxidative programs, as a candidate downstream effector.20 We observed that CMKLR1 overexpression increased the levels of PGC-1α protein, whereas CMKLR1 knockdown had the opposite effect (Figure 5A). To further verify whether CMKLR1 regulates PGC-1α through the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, we treated CMKLR1-overexpressing cells with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002. We noted that pharmacological blockade suppressed the increase in p-PI3K and p-AKT levels induced by CMKLR1 overexpression. Taken together, these findings confirm that PI3K/AKT signaling mediates PGC-1α induction downstream of CMKLR1 (Figure 5B).Fig. 5
CMKLR1 promotes mitochondrial OXPHOS through the PI3K/AKT/PGC-1α axis. (A) Immunoblot analysis of p-PI3K, PI3K, p-AKT, AKT, and PGC-1α in OSCC cells with CMKLR1 knockdown. (B) Protein levels of p-PI3K, p-AKT, and PGC-1α were measured in OSCC cells overexpressing CMKLR1, with or without LY294002 treatment (10 μM). (C) Western blot analysis of representative OXPHOS complex subunits (CI-NDUFB8, CII-SDHB, CIII-UQCRC1, CIV-MTCO2, and CV-ATP5A1) in CMKLR1-overexpressing cells after transfection with siPGC-1α or siNC. (D) Seahorse XF analysis of OCR curves. (E) Quantification of basal respiration, ATP-linked respiration, maximal respiration, and spare respiratory capacity. (F) Representative MitoTracker images and quantification of fluorescence intensity (MitoTracker Red, scale bar = 20 μm). *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 5 dummy alt text

To determine whether PGC-1α is required for CMKLR1-driven mitochondrial respiration, we transfected CMKLR1-overexpressing cells with siRNA targeting PGC-1α (siPGC-1α) or a nontargeting control (siNC). We used immunoblotting and RT-PCR to confirm the depletion of PGC-1α (Figure 5C, Supplementary Figure S2). Our results indicated that PGC-1α silencing significantly attenuated CMKLR1-induced mitochondrial respiration, as evidenced by a reduced OCR and decreased ATP-linked and maximal respiration (Figure 5D and E). Consistently, PGC-1α knockdown diminished the CMKLR1-enhanced MitoTracker Red fluorescence intensity (Figure 5F). Collectively, these findings confirm that CMKLR1 promotes OSCC by activating the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway, increasing the levels of PGC-1α, and sustaining mitochondrial OXPHOS.

sec.title: OXPHOS inhibition attenuates CMKLR1-driven tumor growth
sec.p:
To determine whether the tumor-promoting effects of CMKLR1 are dependent on OXPHOS, we treated CMKLR1-overexpressing OSCC cells with IACS-010759, an inhibitor of complex I. Both CCK-8 and colony formation assays revealed that CMKLR1 overexpression significantly enhanced the proliferation and clonogenic potential of OSCC cells. However, treatment with IACS-010759 markedly suppressed these effects, which in turn reduced cell viability and colony formation to levels comparable to those of the control cells (Figure 6A and B). Transwell invasion and migration assays revealed that IACS-010759 significantly reduced the invasive and migratory capacity of OSCC cells (Figure 6C and D).Fig. 6
Inhibition of OXPHOS reverses the impact of CMKLR1-mediated tumor-promoting effects. (A) CCK-8 assay of the proliferation of CMKLR1-overexpressing (OE) OSCC cells treated with IACS-010759. (B) Colony formation assay of NC, OE, and OE + IACS-010759 cells. The right panel presents the number of colonies. (C, D) Transwell assay revealing significantly impaired cell invasion and migration after OXPHOS inhibitor treatment in CMKLR1-overexpressing cells. Scale bar = 100 μm. (E) Representative images of xenograft tumors derived from NC, OE, and OE + IACS-010759 cells. (F) Tumor growth curves demonstrating tumor volume changes over time. (G) Tumor weight measurements at the endpoint. (H) Representative images of IHC staining of tumor sections with Ki-67. Scale bar = 50 μm. (I) Quantification of Ki67 expression in xenograft tumors. *P < .05; **P < .01; ***P < .001.Fig 6 dummy alt text

To examine whether CMKLR1 promotes OSCC tumor growth through mitochondrial OXPHOS in vivo, we established a subcutaneous xenograft model by using SCC-9 cells stably overexpressing CMKLR1. We observed that mice treated with IACS-010759 exhibited significantly reduced tumor growth (Figure 6E and F). We also noted that the final tumor weights were markedly reduced in the IACS-010759-treated group (Figure 6G). Immunohistochemistry of excised tumor tissues revealed a reduction in Ki-67 staining, which indicated suppressed proliferation (Figure 6H and I). Taken together, these findings suggest that CMKLR1-mediated promotion of OSCC cell growth is, at least in part, dependent on OXPHOS activation.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In this study, we established a link between CMKLR1 and a mitochondrial oxidative phenotype that contributes to aggressive behavior in OSCC. Our results indicate that higher CMKLR1 expression is associated with a poorer prognosis and functionally promotes mitochondrial OXPHOS, which in turn enhances tumor proliferation, invasion, and EMT. Mechanistically, our data support a signaling bridge linking CMKLR1 activity to mitochondrial respiration through a PI3K/AKT/PGC-1α node. Our findings also indicate that pharmacological blockade of mitochondrial complex I reduces CMKLR1-driven tumor growth in vivo. These findings provide novel insights into OSCC metabolic reprogramming and highlight CMKLR1 as a potential therapeutic target.

CMKLR1 has been reported to play divergent roles across various types of cancer, which likely reflects differences in cell context, ligand availability, and immune composition. For example, CMKLR1 has been linked to tumor-promoting programs such as NF-κB activation and matrix-metalloproteinase-related invasiveness in several types of tumors, such as colorectal carcinoma and glioblastoma.15,21,22 By contrast, chemerin/CMKLR1 signaling has been associated with an improved prognosis in patients with lung cancer.23 These context-dependent effects underscore the complexity of CMKLR1 function. In our previous study,13 we reported that the chemerin/CMKLR1 axis plays a role in OSCC progression. We also indicated that chemerin promotes OSCC tumorigenesis and metastasis and that CMKLR1 knockdown inhibits chemerin-induced migration and invasion, with a potential link to oxidative stress pathways (eg, SOD2 activity). In the present study, we extended these observations to delineate a protumorigenic role for CMKLR1 in OSCC. Clinical specimen analysis and functional experiments revealed that higher CMKLR1 expression in tumor tissues was associated with a poorer prognosis for OSCC. Our results also indicated that CMKLR1 knockdown significantly suppressed OSCC cell proliferation, migration, and in vivo tumorigenesis. According to the literature, EMT is often incomplete in OSCC and manifests as partial EMT states that confer a migratory and invasive capacity while retaining certain epithelial features.24 Accordingly, we used EMT-associated markers in this study as supportive molecular readouts to complement functional migration and invasion assays. Although we observed marker shifts consistent with an EMT-like transition, we did not claim a binary, full EMT conversion solely on the basis of marker panels.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to establish a signaling connection between CMKLR1 and mitochondrial bioenergetics. We conducted a quantitative proteomic analysis and observed that CMKLR1 knockdown was associated with broad mitochondrial OXPHOS suppression. According to the literature, abnormal metabolism is a hallmark of cancer. Cancer cells typically modify their metabolic patterns to enhance their growth, invasiveness, and metastasis. OXPHOS dysregulation is associated with poor clinical outcomes in several types of cancer8,25,26 and is linked to the presence of an EMT signature.27 The metabolic functions of CMKLR1 are increasingly being recognized in cancer biology research. For example, genetic or pharmacological inhibition of CMKLR1/GPR1 in clear cell renal cell carcinoma cells has been reported to trigger profound lipid catabolism and cell death, which was reported to reverse the ‘lipid-rich’ phenotype and diminish tumor growth.28 Additionally, high OXPHOS activity has been linked to poor prognosis and recurrence in OSCC, along with resistance to oxidative-stress-induced apoptosis.8 Moreover, TRAP1 has been demonstrated to limit OSCC progression by reducing OXPHOS metabolism in cancer-associated fibroblasts, which suggests that oxidative metabolism in the tumor ecosystem can influence malignant behavior.29 Our findings extend the OSCC OXPHOS literature by revealing CMKLR1 to be an upstream receptor-level determinant of an oxidative bioenergetic program. Our Seahorse assays confirmed that CMKLR1 knockdown significantly reduced the OCR, ATP production rate, and spare respiratory capacity, which indicates that CMKLR1 plays a role in sustaining mitochondrial respiration. Notably, we validated the therapeutic relevance of this axis in vivo. We discovered that utilizing the mitochondrial complex I inhibitor IACS-010759 significantly impaired tumor growth in CMKLR1-overexpressing OSCC xenografts. In previous studies, IACS-010759 has been reported to be efficacious in OXPHOS-dependent models of acute myeloid leukemia and glioblastoma.26,30 Our findings suggest that CMKLR1-high OSCC tumors are metabolically addicted to mitochondrial respiration, which provides a rationale for OXPHOS-targeted interventions in this subset.

Although CMKLR1 has been linked to malignant cancer phenotypes through diverse signaling networks, no studies have yet comprehensively examined how CMKLR1 interfaces with mitochondrial metabolism in OSCC. CMKLR1 is a G-protein-coupled receptor capable of engaging canonical growth pathways, including the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway,31 which is widely implicated in metabolic rewiring and mitochondrial homeostasis. In our study, we observed that CMKLR1 upregulation was accompanied by an increase in PI3K/AKT phosphorylation and an increase in the levels of PGC-1α, a central regulator of mitochondrial oxidative metabolism.20 Notably, treatment with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 suppressed the CMKLR1-induced phosphorylation of AKT and reversed PGC-1α induction, further indicating that CMKLR1 promotes an oxidative bioenergetic state at least in part through PI3K/AKT-dependent regulation of PGC-1α. Genetic depletion of PGC-1α markedly reduced CMKLR1-driven OCR and mitoTraker red signal, which supports a functional requirement for the AKT-PGC-1α node in this context. Overall, these findings extend beyond correlative enrichment analyses and provide mechanistic evidence that CMKLR1 promotes an OXPHOS-dependent malignant phenotype in OSCC. Nevertheless, CMKLR1 signaling is likely multifaceted, and additional downstream pathways (eg, ERK, AMPK, or transcriptional regulators beyond PGC-1α) and ligand-dependent effects (chemerin or resolvin E1) may further shape metabolic states, which warrants future investigation.

Our findings suggest that CMKLR1 can be used as a translational biomarker to identify patients with OSCC who are highly dependent on mitochondrial respiration. In these CMKLR1-high tumors, pharmacological inhibition of OXPHOS, for example, with clinically developed complex I inhibitors such as IACS-010759, may have additional benefits alongside those of conventional surgery, radiotherapy, or chemotherapy. Although our data are preclinical, they support a model in which dual targeting of CMKLR1 signaling and mitochondrial metabolism may overcome metabolic plasticity and limit tumor progression. Future studies involving patient-derived models and larger clinical cohorts are required to validate CMKLR1 as a predictive marker and to optimize OXPHOS-based combination strategies against OSCC. Overall, our findings also suggest that oxidative stress-buffering pathways, including vitamin C- or KLF2–Nrf2-related mechanisms, may influence cellular responses in oral tissues, which should be taken into account when considering the broader consequences of mitochondria-targeted strategies in patients with OSCC.32,33 Because of the known immunomodulatory function of chemerin/CMKLR1 signaling, CMKLR1 may contribute to OSCC progression by regulating the tumor immune microenvironment.

In summary, this study identified a novel CMKLR1-OXPHOS axis that promotes OSCC progression (Figure 7). Targeting CMKLR1 or its downstream metabolic pathways may have a therapeutic benefit for patients with CMKLR1-high tumors.Fig. 7
